violations.claim: "Comparison operators (<=, >=, ==, ...) ... are defined only between two values of the same unit type. Comparing a Voltage to a Current is a compile error ..., not a runtime DRC surprise. This extends naturally to Power, Inductance, Temperature, and Tolerance — e.g. comparing an operating-temperature spec to a tolerance percentage is a compile error, not a nonsensical DRC pass."
violations.problem: The net-annotation grammar slot accepts ANY unit literal and unconditionally wraps it as NetAnnotation::Voltage — nothing at parse, resolve, or expand time checks that the literal is actually Voltage-typed. `net V [85C]: ...` (or [100nF], [5A]) type-checks with zero diagnostics, and every downstream 'voltage' comparison then operates cross-unit on raw femto counts. This also silently corrupts the merged-net contradictory-annotation check (E603), which compares only .femto: a net annotated [5V] in one declaration and [5A] in another compiles clean ('No errors found', reproduced empirically) because 5V and 5A have equal femto — two different unit types treated as identical annotations. This is not a provisional gap-fill: provisional-syntax.md section 4 itself promises 'A non-Voltage unit literal here is a unit-type error (RFC-001's comparison discipline)', so the provisional doc claims the check and the implementation doesn't have it.

A device declaring `spec { voltage_rating: 100nF }` (perfectly legal — device spec fields are free-form name:literal pairs unless a trait constrains them) connected to any voltage-annotated net makes DRC compare a Capacitance against a Voltage; combined with the annotation hole it gets fully absurd: empirically, `voltage_rating: 100nF` on a net annotated [85C] type-checks cleanly and then fires 'D001 voltage-exceed: rated `100nF`, but net `V` is annotated `85C`' — a Capacitance-vs-Temperature comparison presented as a passing/failing voltage check. This is precisely the 'nonsensical DRC' outcome the RFC says must instead be a compile-time unit-type error. On (2), the informal state is mostly coherent (unit lexer/parser codes occupy E101-E111) but has drift worth cleaning when RFC-011 lands: unit-mismatch/bare-number checks at generic sites use E402/E404 (outside E1xx), and the standalone-Unicode-Ω path emits its targeted message under the generic character-error code E001 (src/lex.rs:240-248) while the post-digit path uses E101. Minor quality observation: '10kΩ' (SI prefix + Unicode glyph) yields two diagnostics — E103 '`k` is not one of CoHDL's unit symbols' followed by the targeted 'use `ohm`, not `Ω`' — the RFC-required specific diagnostic is present but arrives as the second error with no combined 'write `10kohm`' help (only the unprefixed '10Ω' form gets the rewrite help); slightly noisy for the repair loop but compliant. Failure mode 1 (plausible-but-wrong prefix, e.g. 100pF for 100nF) is correctly out of scope and indeed not caught. The RFC's comparison-operator claim also mentions in-source `rule` blocks; those are legitimately absent (provisional-syntax.md section 9 cuts in-language rule syntax; the four DRC rules are engine-builtin), so only the engine-builtin comparison surface was audited — and that is where the two violations live. Suggested fix: validate NetAnnotation::Voltage is UnitType::Voltage at parse or expand time, have D001 skip (or better, error on) non-Voltage voltage_rating fields, and route DRC/E603 comparisons through cmp_same_unit with a real (non-debug) unit guard. All 60 existing tests pass (cargo test: 30+11+19 across units/lex/parse unit tests, checker_smoke, exit_criteria); no existing test covers the two violated paths. notes: No violations found: every mechanism RFC-003 claims is actually enforced, and the full test suite (30 tests) passes. Items excluded per 09-mvp-definition.md's cut list: (1) LSP 'find all impls for this device / of this trait' navigation (RFC Tooling & operations) is explicitly cut at 09-mvp-definition.md:59; the underlying queries already exist (World::implemented_traits resolve.rs:77-84, impl_index) so a future LSP has its data. (2) Formal error-code registry is cut at 09-mvp-definition.md:53; the codes exist as stable informal strings and the RFC's actual requirement (two distinct codes) is met. Nuances worth flagging, none rising to violations: (a) 'different module' is realized as 'different file' — MVP has no modules; provisional-syntax.md §1 explicitly maps RFC-003's cross-module organization to cross-file organization in one flat scope, and the std library exercises it (traits in prelude.cohdl, impls grouped elsewhere). (b) Transitive-chain E302s surface one level at a time (each impl checks only its direct bounds, impls.rs:40); a 2-deep missing chain needs two repair iterations, but the invariant — no clean compile with any transitive gap — holds because every indexed impl is itself checked. (c) Anti-cascade choice: has_impl consults impl_index, which is populated before satisfaction checking (resolve.rs:482), so a sibling sub-trait impl that exists but itself fails E301 suppresses the dependent impl's E302 and even lets the dependent impl enter resolved_impls; compile still fails via the sibling's own E301 (empirically verified), and the RFC's stated failure-mode condition is literally 'no impl … anywhere in scope', so this reads as deliberate root-cause-once diagnostics discipline — but it means resolved_impls can transiently contain an impl whose bound chain is broken (harmless today since errors gate artifact emission; a future consumer of resolved_impls on an erroneous World should know). (d) The duplicate-impl test asserts only the E303 code, not the 'earlier location' secondary (tests/checker_smoke.rs:352) — the secondary is emitted (resolve.rs:478, confirmed in rendered output); minor test-coverage thinness, not an enforcement gap. (e) E304/E305 (mapping entry naming a nonexistent trait role/device pin, impls.rs:67-115) and E306 (cyclic sub-trait bounds, resolve.rs:183-198) are consistent gap-fills beyond RFC-003's text; cycle pre-rejection is what makes super_traits_transitive and the E302 machinery terminate. (f) The concrete mapped-body syntax `pins { A: Anode }` is specified by the language spec (10-language-specification.md:124-137), not RFC-003 itself — the implementation matches the spec, and mapping entries may also legally restate same-name pairs (RFC's 'only when names differ' describes when a mapping is needed, not a prohibition; the implementation gives mapping precedence over by-name, impls.rs:120-129).

notes: Method: read RFC-005 in full, audited src/lock.rs line-by-line, cross-checked pipeline.rs/main.rs/ir.rs/resolve.rs/check/expand.rs, ran the full test suite (19/19 pass), and empirically probed three edge cases via a scratch cargo project outside the repo (repo untouched). Letter-vs-spirit items I classified as verified but flag for the parent's judgment: (1) RFC Step 2 says "no shared mutable set threaded through a loop", yet override validation accumulates a mutable `claimed` map through a loop (lock.rs:136-162) — however iteration is over BTreeMaps in canonical path order and the accumulator never feeds fresh numbering, so the v1 order-dependence bug class cannot recur; the fold is equivalent to a pure conflict-detection pass. (2) RFC Step 1 wants the partition "checked as a compile-time invariant on the partition function itself"; the implementation has no dedicated partition function or extra check — exclusivity/totality comes from a single if/else-if/else chain, which is a genuine by-construction language-level guarantee. (3) RFC pseudocode returns Result<_, DuplicateOverrideError>; the implementation instead reports E803 and deterministically poisons the collided override into the fresh group so later errors still surface (lock.rs:156-159) — build still fails and design.lock is never written on error (pipeline.rs:103-107, main.rs:147-152), so poisoned assignments never persist; an MVP-pragmatic diagnostics-recovery elaboration, not a violation. Other observations: the injectivity panic is reachable from a hand-corrupted design.lock (two live paths hand-edited to the same designator → panic labeled "COMPILER BUG", probe-confirmed) — the backstop works, but the message misattributes corrupt user input as a compiler bug; duplicate-value validation in LockState::parse would make the panic truly bug-only (RFC claims no lock-validation mechanism, so not a violation). "Never reusing a tombstoned designator" is enforced for fresh assignment only; an explicit #[designator] override may reuse a tombstoned designator (probe-confirmed: override U1 accepted with tombstone U1 present) — the RFC's Design section explicitly scopes non-reuse to fresh assignment, so this reads as compliant. The override-beats-prior-lock tie-break in Step 1 (lock.rs:126) is unspecified by the RFC but sanctioned by provisional-syntax.md §6 lines 149-150 ("overrides the full designator... resolved before fresh assignment"). Prefix mapping (designator_prefix on traits, lexicographically-smallest declaring trait, default "U") is provisional §6 filling an RFC gap — resolve.rs:62-75 matches it exactly. Tests are golden/fixture-based, not property-based (no proptest/quickcheck dependency); RFC's "Golden-file/property-based tests" is disjunctive and both required shapes (esd/ldo33 same-prefix, order independence) are directly covered, so not a violation. The lock parser is a hand-rolled TOML subset (quoted keys/values, no escape support — lock.rs:91-98), adequate because instance paths are ::-joined identifiers. Per instructions, the informal (unregistered) status of E803/E804 is not reported as a violation — error-code registry formalization is explicitly cut (09-mvp-definition.md:53). Tombstoning is computed slightly earlier than the RFC's "after assignment" phrasing specifically so newly-tombstoned numbers are reserved within the same run (lock.rs:167-173) — strictly stronger than the RFC minimum, with identical observable lock output.

violations.claim: Naming/hygiene: every instance and net produced by expansion, at any nesting depth, gets a unique, deterministic, hierarchical name (Goals bullet 3); collisions 'must be prevented by construction via the call-chain-path naming scheme' (Failure modes)
violations.problem: The mangling namespace (__fn{N}_, __net{N}) is not reserved, so uniqueness is user-forgeable. Proven by probe: (1) a fn-body net literally named __net0 gets key scoped:{path}::__net0 — identical to the key the anonymous-net counter generates in the same scope — so two distinct net declarations silently MERGE into one electrical net (confirmed by giving them contradictory voltage annotations: E603 'net __fn0_f::__net0 has contradictory voltage annotations' fired, proving the merge; without the annotations the design compiles clean with a wrong netlist — the exact 'compiles clean but silently wrong' class this RFC exists to eliminate). (2) At design level, 'net __net0: …' (key named:__net0) plus an anonymous net (key scoped:Board::__net0, display-stripped to __net0) compiles clean and produces two DISTINCT IrNets sharing the emitted name __net0. The RFC's two explicitly enumerated collision classes (cross-call-site instance names; designator allocator input) do hold — instance paths cannot be forged into equality — but the blanket per-net uniqueness guarantee is not 'by construction': no lexer/resolver rule reserves the __ prefix (grep of src/lex.rs, src/parse.rs, src/resolve.rs finds no reserved-identifier handling).

violations.claim: "These two are equivalent — the compiler desugars the first into the second" / "there is exactly ONE trait-bound-checking mechanism in the compiler (the generic-parameter one), not two independent code paths that could silently diverge" (RFC-007 Design + Gradeability; DR-016 Consequences: "Exactly one trait-bound-checking code path exists going forward ... via desugaring"; failure mode 2: "any implementation that lets them diverge is a bug against this RFC's own design")
violations.problem: No desugaring exists. `param: impl Trait` survives as its own AST variant (FnParamTy::ImplTrait, src/ast.rs:325; parsed at parse.rs:784-794) and is checked by a SECOND bound-checking loop in expand.rs:616-660 that duplicates the loop in generics.rs:258-277 instead of routing through resolve_generic_args. Only the underlying trait-satisfaction lookup (world.has_impl -> impl_index over free-standing impls) is shared — which is precisely the structure the RFC criticizes in v1 ("Both call the same underlying trait-satisfaction lookup" yet counted as two mechanisms). The two paths' diagnostics have already diverged in wording: named-generic path says "required by `D`" with help "add `impl X for Y { … }` (checked at the impl statement, RFC-003), or pass a device that has one" (generics.rs:264-273); impl-Trait path says "required by parameter `target` of fn `add_decoupling`" with a shorter help (expand.rs:629-637) — confirmed empirically via scratch fixtures f3/f4. Additionally the two forms are not call-site interchangeable as literal desugaring would imply: a named trait-bound parameter requires an explicit turbofish argument (E401 if omitted, generics.rs:66-79 — no inference), while the impl-Trait form takes none (the turbofish asymmetry itself is pinned by provisional-syntax.md §8, so it is a provisional choice, but it underlines that 'pure sugar' is not what is implemented). Compounding the mismatch, the in-repo docs restate the unimplemented mechanism: src/check/generics.rs:1-5 module header claims impl-Trait params "(desugared) all resolve through `resolve_generic_args`" (false), and provisional-syntax.md §8 says "impl Trait (desugared per RFC-007)". Observable accept/reject behavior and the E403 code/diagnostic discipline are currently equivalent (both check every bound via world.has_impl, both bind via_traits identically for role access — expand.rs:642-653 vs 575-594), so nothing is dormant — but the mechanism the RFC/DR-016 claim (one code path kept honest by desugaring) is not the mechanism that exists, and the maintained-in-parallel divergence risk the RFC set out to eliminate is present, with message-level divergence already realized.
